newsitem.title: PERU: Loud bang shatters calm in Peru hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Loud bang shatters calm in Peru hostage crisis.

text.p: A loud explosion in the middle of the night shattered a Christmas lull on Thursday at the Japanese embassy residence in Peru, where armed Marxist guerrillas were holding 104 VIP hostages for a ninth day.

Police watching from a distance were unable to say what had happened or whether any of the captives, who include ambassadors and top government officials, had been hurt. No damage to the outside of the building was visible.

Spokesman Roland Bigler told a news conference the Red Cross had not received reports of injuries to the hostages but could not be certain no one was hurt as none of its delegates had entered the building. The organisation believes the blast was set off by an animal, he said, without giving details.

Released hostages have said the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels who are holding the residence are armed with grenades, explosives and large stocks of ammunition and have booby-trapped entrances to the grand two-floor building. One local newspaper speculated that the blast, at 1:43 A.M. (0643 GMT), might have come when a cat or rat stepped on a mine planted by the rebels.

"I was asleep on the sidewalk nearby along with other reporters and then suddenly this explosion woke me," Reuters photographer Claudia Daut said. "It was loud. We all jumped to our feet. Police were shouting at us to get down on the ground."

Reporters were unable to see clearly what was happening in the pitch darkness but detected police in dark clothes moving around in the streets outside the residence, Daut said. A Red Cross official ran from his night watch post after the explosion to call for the immediate presence of a top Red Cross official.
But as there were no further incidents or requests from the rebels for a representative to enter the building, the Red Cross said it had not entered the residence.

The explosion came hours after the rebels freed a sick Japanese hostage and allowed the other 104 to enjoy a Catholic Mass and a turkey Christmas lunch sent by President Alberto Fujimori. The released man, Kenji Hirata, 34, his head slumped to one side, was pushed out of the residence in a wheelchair by Red Cross workers on Wednesday.

A police ambulance sped Hirata, a first secretary at the Japanese embassy in Lima, to a nearby hospital, where he was placed on an intravenous drip and treated for dehydration. The Red Cross said his condition was stable, but relatives in Japan said they were worried about his health.

Hirata's release was the first since Uruguayan Ambassador Tabare Bocalandro's on Tuesday after his government freed two MRTA guerrillas from jail. Furious at the apparent concession, Peru recalled its top diplomat from Uruguay and Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto also criticised the apparent swap.

"The Uruguay government has explained that there was no link between the two (release of the two rebels and the Lima hostage issue)," Hashimoto told reporters in Tokyo. "I don't know whether this is true or not but in any case it has made a solution of the case difficult," he said. "We must not surrender to terrorism."

Japan has about 30 nationals in the besieged residence, including Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, host of the ill-fated cocktail reception stormed by the rebels. In a sign Tokyo expects the crisis to drag on, Foreign Ministry officials said Japan's prime minister and foreign minister were both considering cancelling foreign trips planned for January.

Fujimori has flatly rejected all the demands made by the guerrillas and said they must release the captives and hand over their weapons. He has also turned down foreign offers of military help. But Russian President Boris Yeltsin's suggestion on Wednesday of sending a special Group of Seven task force to free the hostages brought no immediate response from Lima.

The rebels have vowed not to surrender until the government releases more than 400 MRTA members from Peruvian jails. They also want an end to free-market economic policies and more state support for the impoverished majority of the country's majority.

Japanese media covering the crisis speculated a behind-the-scenes deal might be worked out to allow the MRTA captors to fly to asylum in Cuba after releasing the hostages, but there has been no official word on this possibility.
Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi arrived in Lima early on Thursday to try to secure the release of his country's ambassador to Peru, Ahmad Mokhtar.
